title: The harvest (Revelation 14)
hook: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; they rest from their labors
tomorrow: The song of Moses and the Lamb

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beasts: one from the sea that wanted worship, one with a lamb's horns and a dragon's voice. Your line was don't bow to the beast. Where did you say no? Day one thousand three hundred six.

A funeral, on a gray afternoon. People in dark coats stand around an open grave. The minister opens a worn book and reads a few lines that sound older than everyone there: a voice from heaven, telling John to write something down. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. They rest from their labors. And their works follow them. Those words come from the middle of Revelation fourteen, a chapter full of angels flying, a sickle, and a field ready to be cut. Today's word is that field: the harvest.

First, the chapter opens on a mountain. The Lamb stands on Mount Sion with his people, and they sing a new song no one else can learn. After the beasts of yesterday, the Lamb is still standing. Second, the voice. In the King James words: "Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them." Notice the order. Rest first. Then, their works follow them. Nothing good they did is lost; it goes along behind them like a family walking behind a coffin. The old Anglican Book of Common Prayer sets this verse in its burial service, read at the grave. Third, the harvest itself. John sees one "like unto the Son of man," sitting on a white cloud with a sharp sickle, and an angel calls out: "Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe." Jesus told stories like this: wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest. Here the harvest comes. A second harvest follows, of grapes thrown into a winepress, and it's a hard picture of judgment. Some readers take it literally; others hear it as picture language. Fourth, for anyone who has buried someone who died in faith, the chapter says two things at once: those who die in the Lord are at rest, and their works are not left behind. The harvest is the time when what was growing is finally gathered in.

Here's the practice: pray for your dead, or remember them if you don't pray. Settle, and breathe. Let one person who has died come to mind. A grandparent. A friend. Someone you never got to say goodbye to. See their face. Then think of one good thing they did that's still following them: a recipe you still cook, a habit of kindness, a phrase you catch yourself saying. If you pray, you can commend them to God by name, and ask that they rest. If you don't, just thank them silently. If another name comes, let it come. The bell holds the time.
The harvest. In Revelation fourteen, the field of the earth gathered in at the end, and the dead who die in the Lord at rest, with their works following them.
Your line: they rest from their labors. Today, do one small thing the way someone you've lost used to do it, and let their works follow them a little further. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians pray for or remember their dead at funerals and on days set aside for them, and Revelation 14:13 is read in some burial services; churches differ on praying for the dead, with Catholic and Orthodox Christians praying for them directly and some Protestants giving thanks for them instead.

fork.reveal: the Spirit says they rest from their labors, and their works follow them. rest first, and the good they did goes with them.

original.note: Greek: harvest, reaping. the word for the ripe harvest of the earth in Revelation 14:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grim reaper with a sickle.
what it means: the earth's harvest gathered in, and the dead in the Lord at rest, their good works following them.
what a scholar hears: the sickle and the ripe field echo the harvest image in Jesus's parables and in the prophet Joel.
